turns.content: I thought flaps just made the wing bigger. Is that all they do?

Flaps primarily work by changing the camber of the airfoil, which increases the wing's lift coefficient. Some flap designs also increase the surface area of the wing, but the camber change is the primary mechanism. Because lift depends on the lift coefficient along with air density, velocity, and surface area, increasing the lift coefficient directly increases lift.

turns.content: On my checkride, the examiner asked whether flaps change the critical angle of attack. What is the correct answer?

Flap deflection does not increase the critical angle of attack. In some cases, flap deflection actually decreases the critical angle of attack. This is an important distinction because while flaps increase the lift coefficient, the stall AOA does not go up and may actually be reduced depending on flap design.

turns.content: Flaps and ailerons both deflect wing surfaces, so they should produce similar rolling effects, right?

Not quite. Ailerons deflect asymmetrically, creating asymmetrical lift that produces a rolling moment about the longitudinal axis. Flaps, by contrast, act symmetrically about the longitudinal axis, so they produce no rolling moment. Both lift and drag increase with flap deflection, along with a pitching moment about the lateral axis.

turns.content: Why do flaps cause the airplane to pitch? I expected the nose to just stay level.

Flap deflection causes a pitching moment primarily because of the rearward movement of the wing's center of pressure. However, the actual pitch behavior depends on several variables including flap type, wing position, downwash behavior, and horizontal tail location. The airplane may pitch nose-up, nose-down, or show minimal pitch change depending on the specific design.

turns.content: Can you explain the drag difference between small and large flap deflections?

Flap deflection up to 15 degrees primarily produces lift with minimal increases in drag. Beyond 15 degrees, there is a large increase in drag. That drag is parasite drag, which is proportional to the square of the speed. So at higher speeds, the drag penalty from large flap deflections becomes significantly greater.

Lift is a function of air density, velocity, surface area, and lift coefficient. Flaps contribute by increasing the lift coefficient and, with some designs, also increasing the surface area. All four variables work together to determine the total lift generated by the wing.

turns.content: My instructor mentioned something about downwash and high-wing airplanes with flaps. What does that mean?

When flaps are deflected beyond 15 degrees, the resulting downwash changes the airflow over the horizontal tail. In most high-wing airplanes, this produces a significant nose-up pitching moment. The horizontal tail's location relative to the wing's downwash field is one of the design variables that determines how the airplane pitches when flaps are extended.

turns.content: Since parasite drag is proportional to the square of speed, does that mean flap drag is especially significant at cruise speeds?

Yes, that relationship is important. Parasite drag from flap deflection is proportional to the square of the speed, so at higher speeds the drag penalty increases rapidly. This is one reason flaps have maximum extension speeds and are not used at cruise. The drag effect becomes much more pronounced as speed increases.

No, not always. As flaps are deflected, the aircraft may pitch nose-up, nose-down, or have minimal changes in pitch attitude. However, deflection beyond 15 degrees does produce a significant nose-up pitching moment in most high-wing airplanes due to downwash effects on the horizontal tail.

turns.content: How would you explain to an examiner why flaps are useful for landing even though they increase drag?

Flaps increase the wing's lift coefficient by changing airfoil camber, which allows the airplane to maintain lift at lower airspeeds. This enables a slower, more controlled approach and landing. The increased drag is actually useful on approach because it helps steepen the descent path and slow the airplane without requiring a large reduction in engine power, giving the pilot better control.

turns.content: What exactly is camber and why does changing it matter for lift?

Camber refers to the curvature of the airfoil's mean line from leading edge to trailing edge. When flaps are deflected, they increase the camber of the wing, which increases the lift coefficient. Since lift depends on the lift coefficient along with air density, velocity, and surface area, a higher lift coefficient means more lift is generated at any given speed.

turns.content: I understand flaps increase both lift and drag, but do they affect both axes equally?

No. Flaps produce a pitching moment about the lateral axis due to the rearward shift of the wing's center of pressure and downwash effects on the tail. About the longitudinal axis, flaps act symmetrically and produce no rolling moment. Ailerons, by contrast, create asymmetrical lift and do produce a rolling moment about the longitudinal axis.

Sure! Plain flaps increase lift with minimal drag. Split flaps provide more lift and drag, useful for landing. Slotted flaps enhance lift by delaying airflow separation, improving takeoff and climb. Fowler flaps increase wing area and lift, common in larger aircraft.
